title: The Global Contribution of Polycrisis Resilience Through 2100
subtitle: A Theoretical and Quantitative Assessment of Hunter Hughes’s Framework for Saving Lives, Mitigating Person-Years of Human Suffering, Protecting Nearly 5 Billion At-Risk People, and Avoiding Trillions in Economic Losses (2026–2100)
description: A prospective, scenario-based assessment of what Polycrisis Resilience could achieve by 2100 and how much of that could be attributed to the framework itself: five attribution tiers, six capacities and a 5,000-run uncertainty analysis.
contribution: A prospective, scenario-based estimate of the framework’s possible contribution to 2100, separating a global resilience envelope from a small attributable share across five tiers, and stating that all figures are scenarios, not historical outcomes.
abstract: This report presents a theoretical and quantitative assessment of the long-term global significance of Polycrisis Resilience, a framework developed and formalized by Hunter Hughes in 2026 through H Heuristics. The study examines how the establishment of an operational resilience doctrine for interconnected global crises could influence human welfare, mortality reduction, climate adaptation, economic development, and vulnerability reduction through the year 2100. Distinguishing between the broader global benefits of coordinated resilience investments and the marginal contribution attributable to the framework itself, the report develops a transparent counterfactual attribution model incorporating five sensitivity tiers ranging from 0.01% to 10% influence.

Using the HH-PRM v2.0-ATTR model, the analysis estimates a global Polycrisis Resilience envelope of 368 million premature deaths prevented, 221 billion person-years of reduced human suffering, protection for up to 4.8 billion people exposed to compounding risks, and US$200 trillion to US$296 trillion in avoided economic losses between 2026 and 2100. Attributable outcomes associated with the dissemination and adoption of the Polycrisis Resilience framework range from hundreds of thousands of lives saved under conservative assumptions to tens of millions under higher adoption scenarios. The study further evaluates impacts across air pollution reduction, extreme heat adaptation, water security, healthcare access, economic convergence, and multi-generational resilience outcomes.

The report concludes that establishing an accessible, development-oriented framework for navigating interacting global crises during the critical 2026-2035 investment decade has the potential to influence policy priorities, accelerate proactive action, and enhance resilience across multiple generations. All impact estimates are explicitly presented as prospective counterfactual scenarios rather than historical outcomes and are evaluated through uncertainty analysis, sensitivity testing, and Monte Carlo simulations to maintain transparency regarding assumptions and future realization conditions.
coreProposition: By establishing the operational concept of Polycrisis Resilience online in 2026, with 74 years remaining in the century, the report argues that a publicly accessible framework could help save lives, mitigate person-years of suffering and avoid economic losses by 2100. All figures are prospective counterfactual scenarios, not historical outcomes.

keyFindings.title: The global envelope is large.
keyFindings.text: Full implementation of coordinated polycrisis resilience (Scenario S3, costing about 1% of world GDP) is estimated to prevent 368 million premature deaths (90% uncertainty interval 265–448 million), gain 13.6 billion healthy life-years and deliver 221 billion person-years of improved survivability conditions between 2026 and 2100.

keyFindings.title: About 136 million lives depend on coordination.
keyFindings.text: Funding single-crisis programmes in silos (Scenario S2) is estimated to save 232 million lives, leaving 136 million preventable deaths that only cross-sector design could address.

keyFindings.title: Delay is costly in the model.
keyFindings.text: The model puts the cost of a year of global delay at 8.3 million preventable deaths. Under that assumption, accelerating mobilization by 32 days would correspond to 368,000 lives, and by 5.3 months to 1.84 million.

keyFindings.title: Suffering concentrates in air pollution and heat.
keyFindings.text: The largest contributions to reduced suffering are air pollution reduction (92 billion person-years) and extreme-heat and climate protection (118 billion person-years).

keyFindings.title: Demographic pressure.
keyFindings.text: Population growth in climate-exposed regions, led by Sub-Saharan Africa (1.3 billion to 3.5 billion) and South Asia, projects about 4.85 billion people into high survivability risk by 2100 without proactive investment in 2026–2035.

keyFindings.title: The attributable share is a scenario parameter.
keyFindings.text: The report separates the global envelope from the share attributable to the framework’s creation and dissemination, modelled in five tiers from 0.01% to 10%: 36,800 lives at the lowest tier, 368,000 at 0.1%, and 3.7 to 36.8 million at the highest tiers.

keyFindings.title: Economic scale.
keyFindings.text: Against an estimated dividend of about US$4 trillion a year (US$200 to 296 trillion over the century), the attributable avoided losses range from US$200 billion at a 0.1% share to US$10 to 29.6 trillion at the highest tiers.

keyFindings.title: Realization conditions.
keyFindings.text: The authors list conditions for any of this to occur: sustained discoverability, independent scholarly engagement and critique, integration into green-transition appraisal, institutional adoption, empirical validation of the metrics, and curriculum diffusion. A 5,000-run Monte Carlo analysis shows uncertainty bounds for each tier.
